paras: The attempted lynching of the Gordon brothers was a failed attempt by a mob at Vincennes, Indiana, to take two Black brothers named Gordon out of jail and hang them some time between October 1881 and April 1882. The brothers, accused of robbing an elderly couple, were saved by the sheriff and later convicted, after which a third brother declared that he and an uncle had committed the crime.

According to Der Westbote, a German-language paper in Columbus, Ohio, two armed men climbed through the window of Wilhelm Kröger, a 60-year-old market dealer, and his 50-year-old wife about two miles east of Vincennes at 2 a.m. on the night of October 5-6, 1881. The intruders clubbed both of them senseless, took fifteen dollars, and escaped as Kröger fired two shots after them. Sheriff Hackley soon arrested two Black men ("Neger"), whom the paper named Andrew and Cortland Gordon, and the Krögers identified them as the robbers.
The robbery caused great excitement among the Germans of the neighborhood, and threats were made to "lynch" the accused.

A later wire brief, which named the brothers Harry and Curtland Gordon, reported that a mob tried to take them out of jail and hang them but "were baffled by a plucky Sheriff." The brief gave no date, time or size for the mob, and no injuries were reported.

The brothers were tried and found guilty a few days before the brief appeared in April 1882. Their brother Joe then declared that he and an uncle were the guilty ones, saying he had meant to stay silent if his brothers were acquitted but would not let them go to state prison. Joe also said he had been present at the attempted lynching and would have spoken then if it had been necessary; no report of how his statement was resolved was found.

Der Westbote reported the robbery in October 1881 as an outrage against local Germans and remarked that it would be no pity if short work were made of the Gordons, whom it called hardened rogues. The English-language wire brief, printed in the Raleigh Farmer and Mechanic on April 12, 1882, named no race, credited the sheriff and centered on the brother's confession.

The two reports differ on one brother's first name, Andrew in Der Westbote and Harry in the wire brief. They also leave guilt in dispute: the Krögers identified the Gordons and a jury convicted them, but their brother Joe named himself and an uncle as the robbers.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of the Gordon brothers at Vincennes, Indiana
bases: A mob tried to take two jailed prisoners out and hang them but was stopped by the sheriff (A2), after lynching threats had been made following their arrest (A1).
No one was killed: the mob that tried to take the Gordons from jail to hang them was turned back by the sheriff (A2); the episode is an attempted lynching over a robbery accusation (A1, A2).
The jail attempt appears only in one wire brief (A2, reprinted A3); the German-language report (A1) independently confirms the robbery, the arrests and lynching threats but predates the attempt.

info: The robbery took place about 2 a.m. on the night of October 5-6, 1881; the date of the jail attempt is not reported.
Vincennes, Ind.; the robbed couple lived about two miles east of the town.
Two brothers named Gordon, described as Black ("Neger"): Andrew and Cortland Gordon in A1; Harry and Curtland Gordon in A2.
Accused of breaking into the home of Wilhelm Kröger, 60, and his wife, 50, clubbing both and taking fifteen dollars.
A mob of unstated size and make-up; earlier threats to lynch came from Germans of the neighborhood.
After the verdict their brother Joe declared that he and an uncle were the guilty ones; no later report of the outcome was found.
